title: Northstar Support Platform - onboarding friction + production readiness feedback
summary: Northstar shared detailed friction points from their first-week Hosted API trial: confusion around which API key to use and env var naming leading to 401/403, uncertainty on what a "successful" first request should look like (non-streaming vs streaming), surprise 429s when they switched from a curl test to a small load test, and confusion when usage dashboards lagged. They asked Redwood to provide clearer "production readiness" steps (timeouts/retries, idempotency guidance, streaming reconnect, quotas/budget alerts, model pinning/fallback) and requested these be surfaced in Console rather than scattered across docs.
topics: 429 rate limit surprise during initial load test
Usage dashboard delay and perceived mismatch with requests
What a 'go-live checklist' should include (quotas, budgets, model pinning, fallback policy, observability hooks)
questions: Can we have one canonical checklist for "first production launch" that our team can follow and sign off on?
What are the recommended default timeouts/retry policies for the SDKs (and do they differ for streaming)?
How do we set quotas/budgets to avoid accidental spend during early tests?
Is there an expected delay on the usage dashboard, and where do we verify ground truth during that window?
action_items: Wei Chen (Redwood) - Send Northstar the draft 'First production launch' checklist steps + canonical docs links (auth/env var, first request, streaming, retries, quotas/budgets, usage dashboard) - Due 2025-02-10
Sabrina James (Redwood) - Share a production-ready curl + SDK snippet showing timeouts/retries and streaming reconnect guidance (language-agnostic plus Python/TS pointers) - Due 2025-02-13
Ben Carter (Redwood) - Follow up with pricing/plan info for higher initial quota / dedicated burst options and how rate limits are communicated - Due 2025-02-12
Maya Desai (Northstar) - Provide timestamps + request IDs for their 401/403 and 429 examples so Redwood can validate eventing and recommend settings - Due 2025-02-07
next_steps: Redwood to email Northstar a consolidated onboarding + production readiness checklist draft and ask for redlines
Northstar to run a repeat test with updated recommended retry/backoff and confirm whether 429 behavior is expected for their tier
Schedule a 30-min follow-up to review checklist + discuss options for predictable throughput (higher limits vs Dedicated)
transcript:
Meeting Header
Date: 2025-02-06
Time: 5:00pm - 5:44pm PT
Duration: 44 minutes
Title: Northstar Support Platform - onboarding friction + production readiness feedback
Attendees:
- Ben Carter (Redwood Inference)
- Sabrina James (Redwood Inference)
- Wei Chen (Redwood Inference)
- Maya Desai (Northstar Support Platform)
- Jordan Lee (Northstar Support Platform)
- Priya Natarajan (Northstar Support Platform)

Auto-Summary (generated)
- Customer trialed Hosted API and hit multiple early friction points.
- Customer wants an explicit production checklist (not just quickstart snippets).
- Redwood to follow up with docs consolidation + SDK guidance on retries/timeouts/streaming.


[00:00] Ben Carter: Alright, cool. Thanks everyone for making time. Uh, the goal today is basically to hear what was painful in the first week, right? Like, what slowed you down from first call to actually putting even a tiny amount of prod-ish traffic through.

[00:16] Maya Desai: Yeah, that’s exactly it. We did get it working, but it was like… way more back-and-forth than it should be.

[00:24] Ben Carter: Yep. And just to level-set, you’re on Hosted API right now, correct?

[00:28] Priya Natarajan: Correct. We’re evaluating for our support agent assist feature.

[00:32] Ben Carter: Perfect. Sabrina’s on as well, she can go deep on SDK behavior, and Wei from docs since a lot of this tends to be “where do I even find the right page.”

[00:41] Wei Chen: Hey everyone.

[00:43] Sabrina James: Hey.

[00:46] Ben Carter: Maya, do you wanna start with what happened when you tried the quickstart?

[00:51] Maya Desai: Sure. So the first thing is, we followed the quickstart, I think it was like “create an API key, set REDWOOD_API_KEY,” something like that, and then our first few calls were 401.

[01:03] Jordan Lee: Yeah, and the error message was not… it’s not super obvious. It’s like “invalid auth token” and we weren’t sure if we picked the wrong key or if it was like workspace vs project.

[01:15] Ben Carter: Got it. 401 invalid key. Was it actually the wrong key, or env var not set?

[01:20] Jordan Lee: It was both, kind of. We generated a key but then we copied a different key from another tab. And then our CI env var was named REDWOOD_KEY, not REDWOOD_API_KEY. So locally it worked, then it didn’t in our test job.

[01:35] Maya Desai: And the docs have like two pages that talk about keys. One in Console and one in the API reference. We weren’t sure which was canonical.

[01:43] Wei Chen: That’s helpful. So you saw inconsistent naming and multiple entry points. Did you see 403 at all, like forbidden, org not allowed?

[01:52] Jordan Lee: Yeah, briefly. We had a key that was… I think scoped? Or maybe it got rotated. I don’t remember. We saw 403 and then 401. We ended up regenerating and then it worked.

[02:03] Sabrina James: Do you remember if you were hitting the right base URL? Sometimes people use the OpenAI compat URL with Redwood key or vice versa.

[02:10] Jordan Lee: Oh, yes. That too. We used the OpenAI-style endpoint first because our internal wrapper assumes it. Then we swapped to the Redwood endpoint. That was part of the confusion.

[02:21] Ben Carter: Okay, that’s a very common path. So basically: key + env var naming + endpoint mismatch.

[02:29] Priya Natarajan: From a product side, it was like: we want one “do this first” path that doesn’t branch into five different docs.

[02:38] Ben Carter: Makes sense. Once you got past auth, did you get to a first successful response quickly?

[02:43] Maya Desai: We did, but then we got stuck again when we tried streaming. The non-streaming example worked. Streaming kept disconnecting and we didn’t know if we had to handle reconnects or if Redwood would resume.

[02:57] Jordan Lee: Yeah the stream just ends and you get partial output, and we were like, is that our network, or is that rate limiting, or is that expected?

[03:06] Sabrina James: Was it like an SSE stream? And you were using your own HTTP client?

[03:11] Jordan Lee: We used our own, yeah. We didn’t pull in the SDK at first. We just did fetch in Node.

[03:18] Sabrina James: Got it. So, we generally recommend the SDK for streaming because it handles some edge cases—like when the connection drops mid-generation you need to decide whether to retry and how you dedupe. But we haven’t been super explicit in docs about what “production safe streaming” looks like.

[03:34] Maya Desai: Right, and that’s really the theme. Like, the quickstart gets you a happy path. Then production has a bunch of “okay but what about” steps.

[03:45] Ben Carter: Yeah. That’s exactly why we’re doing these calls. What were the other “okay but what abouts”?

[03:52] Maya Desai: Rate limits. We did a tiny load test, nothing crazy, like we replayed 20 chats at once, and then we started getting 429.

[04:01] Priya Natarajan: And I’ll just say it: it freaked our leadership out. Because they’re like “if this happens on day one, it’s not ready.”

[04:07] Ben Carter: Totally fair. What plan are you on right now? Like the self-serve trial tier?

[04:12] Jordan Lee: Yeah, trial with credits.

[04:14] Ben Carter: Okay, so the 429 is expected if you exceed the trial quota. But we should do a better job of explaining what limits apply and what a backoff policy should be.

[04:26] Jordan Lee: The response didn’t tell us what to do. Like it didn’t give a “retry-after” that we noticed.

[04:31] Sabrina James: We do include Retry-After on some routes but it might not be consistent. Also if you’re behind a proxy you might not see it. I don’t want to guess; if you can send one example header set we can confirm.

[04:44] Maya Desai: Yeah. And we didn’t know what to implement. Exponential backoff? jitter? How many retries before fail? What timeout? Like, we don’t want to melt you or ourselves.

[04:56] Ben Carter: Makes sense. This is actually one of the things we’re tightening: recommended defaults per SDK.

[05:03] Wei Chen: And docs wise, I think we need a single “Production readiness” page that includes: timeouts, retries, streaming reconnect patterns, idempotency.

[05:12] Priya Natarajan: Plus budgets and quotas. Because we also had the opposite fear: if we remove the rate limit, do we just blow through spend?

[05:21] Ben Carter: Yeah, budgets/quotas guardrails.

[05:23] Jordan Lee: We couldn’t figure out where to set that. We found “limits” in Console but it wasn’t clear if it was per key or per org.

[05:31] Ben Carter: Today it’s org/workspace level. We can walk you through it, but longer term we want it surfaced in a checklist.

[05:40] Maya Desai: This is the ask: can you give us a checklist that’s like “to go live, do these 8 things.” Not a blog post. A checkbox list.

[05:51] Ben Carter: That is very aligned with what we’re building. So, if we did that, what would you want on it?

[05:58] Maya Desai: Start with “make first request” but the real stuff is: set correct key, confirm environment variables, test streaming, set timeouts/retries, set quotas/budget alerts, confirm usage dashboard, pin a model version, and… I don’t know, like a fallback?

[06:15] Jordan Lee: Yeah fallback policy. Like if the model is overloaded or whatever, can you failover? Or at least what are best practices.

[06:23] Ben Carter: We can do fallbacks in a couple ways. In Hosted you can specify a primary and a compatible fallback, or you can implement client-side.

[06:32] Jordan Lee: That’s the thing. We didn’t know that existed.

[06:35] Wei Chen: That’s on us. It’s documented but not discoverable.

[06:40] Sabrina James: Also, from the SDK perspective, we can bake in recommended timeouts and retry behavior so you don’t have to reinvent it. Right now it’s more “bring your own HTTP client config.”

[06:53] Maya Desai: Please do. Because our engineers will not all implement it the same way.

[06:58] Ben Carter: Yep. Okay. Let me ask about the “first success” moment. What did you consider success internally?

[07:05] Priya Natarajan: We wanted: a request from our staging environment, using our prompt template, getting a response we can parse, and see it show up in the usage dashboard so Finance can see spend.

[07:17] Jordan Lee: And that last part didn’t work right away. The usage dashboard didn’t update for a while.

[07:23] Ben Carter: How long?

[07:24] Jordan Lee: Like, 20 minutes? We weren’t sure. It might’ve been longer.

[07:29] Maya Desai: We thought our requests weren’t being counted. So we ran more. Which is the worst possible behavior.

[07:36] Ben Carter: Yeah. That’s a classic trap. There is some lag. We should set expectations and also provide a “ground truth” view for immediate confirmation.

[07:45] Wei Chen: We have request logs in Console that are more real-time, but again, it’s not something a new user finds.

[07:51] Priya Natarajan: Exactly. If it’s a checklist, one step could be “verify in request logs” and the next “verify usage dashboard within X minutes.”

[08:02] Sabrina James: And maybe even: “don’t re-run load tests to confirm billing.”

[08:06] Jordan Lee: Yeah, seriously.

[08:09] Ben Carter: Let me capture the main friction points: auth setup, endpoint confusion, streaming disconnects/no guidance, rate limit surprises and no clear backoff defaults, and usage dashboard lag.

[08:23] Maya Desai: That’s basically it.

[08:25] Ben Carter: Anything around security/compliance yet? Or too early.

[08:29] Priya Natarajan: Too early. But we will need audit logs and SSO if we proceed. For now we just want to get a pilot stable.

[08:38] Ben Carter: Okay. And timeline wise, are you trying to get something in production this quarter?

[08:44] Priya Natarajan: Ideally yes. We’re aiming for a small rollout in March.

[08:49] Ben Carter: Great.

[08:50] Sabrina James: Can I ask on the streaming disconnect: was it happening consistently or sporadically?

[08:56] Jordan Lee: Sporadic. Like 1 out of 10. Which makes it harder.

[09:00] Sabrina James: That sounds like network intermediary or client timeout rather than server always. What timeout did you set?

[09:06] Jordan Lee: Whatever default fetch has. So… none? Or some default.

[09:12] Sabrina James: Yeah, so we should be explicit. For streaming, you want a higher idle timeout, but you also want a total request cap. And then if it fails mid-stream, you need to decide whether to restart the whole completion. There’s no magical resume unless you have an idempotency key plus some server support.

[09:31] Jordan Lee: Exactly. We need a recommended pattern.

[09:34] Wei Chen: We can add a “Streaming in production” page with reconnect patterns and caveats.

[09:41] Maya Desai: I’d love that. But honestly, I’d love it even more if the Console pointed me to it at the moment I’m setting up.

[09:49] Ben Carter: Like in-product checklist.

[09:51] Maya Desai: Yes. Like, “Step 3: Try streaming. Here’s what can go wrong.”

[09:58] Ben Carter: Understood.

[10:00] Priya Natarajan: The other thing is, the wording “first successful request” is ambiguous. Like success for you might be any 200. For us success is a request using our actual integration and guardrails.

[10:14] Ben Carter: That’s a good point. Maybe we split: “First API call” vs “First production-safe call.”

[10:20] Wei Chen: Or “Hello world” vs “Production readiness.”

[10:23] Jordan Lee: Yes.

[10:25] Ben Carter: Okay. Let’s talk about rate limits briefly. When you hit 429, what did your client do?

[10:31] Jordan Lee: We didn’t have retries. We just failed. Then we tried a couple manual reruns.

[10:36] Sabrina James: The SDKs can automatically retry 429 with exponential backoff and jitter. We just need to make that the default or at least an obvious preset.

[10:46] Jordan Lee: That’s what we want. Because we’re not going to implement it per team.

[10:51] Maya Desai: And include it in the snippet. Like, the snippet should show it.

[10:55] Wei Chen: Agreed. Right now snippets are too “toy.”

[10:58] Ben Carter: Are you primarily Node or Python?

[11:01] Jordan Lee: Node/TypeScript in the backend. Some Python for evals.

[11:05] Ben Carter: Great. We can get you a TypeScript snippet with recommended defaults.

[11:10] Sabrina James: Also, are you using the OpenAI compatibility layer in production, or are you willing to use the native Redwood SDK?

[11:17] Jordan Lee: We’d prefer compat because our abstraction is built around that, but we can change if needed.

[11:23] Ben Carter: You can stay on compat. We just need to make sure the docs say “if you use compat, set these headers, use these endpoints, and here’s how to tag requests.”

[11:33] Jordan Lee: Yeah.

[11:35] Wei Chen: One thing I want to ask: when you were trying to find docs, did you search or navigate from Console?

[11:43] Maya Desai: We started in Console. But it’s like: I click docs and then I’m in a big docs site. Search results were not great for “401 invalid key.”

[11:54] Wei Chen: Noted.

[11:55] Ben Carter: Okay. Let me switch gears slightly. When you think “production readiness,” what would you want to show your internal stakeholders?

[12:03] Priya Natarajan: A screenshot or export that says we completed steps. Like, “quotas set, logging enabled, model pinned.” We have to do internal review.

[12:12] Maya Desai: Yeah. Honestly a checklist in the Console would be perfect.

[12:16] Ben Carter: That’s helpful. We’re building something like that.

[12:19] Jordan Lee: One more pain: model selection. We picked a model from the catalog, but then we weren’t sure if that model version could change. Like, do you upgrade under us?

[12:29] Ben Carter: Good question. You can pin model versions. By default we may move “latest” forward, but you can pin.

[12:36] Jordan Lee: That should be like step 6. “Pin model version.”

[12:40] Wei Chen: Agreed.

[12:42] Sabrina James: And if you pin, you also need a plan for fallback. Like if the pinned model is temporarily unavailable.

[12:49] Maya Desai: Exactly.

[12:51] Ben Carter: Okay.

[12:52] (crosstalk)

[12:53] Priya Natarajan: Also, cost. Not in detail yet, but we want to know how to avoid accidental spend.

[13:00] Ben Carter: Yeah. Budgets and alerts.

[13:03] Jordan Lee: Is there a webhook for usage?

[13:06] Ben Carter: There are alert integrations and we have examples; we can send you a Terraform snippet and also a manual path in Console.

[13:14] Jordan Lee: Cool.

[13:16] Ben Carter: Let’s do this: Wei, can you send them a consolidated page or at least a draft checklist and links? I know it’s not fully published.

[13:24] Wei Chen: Yeah, I can send a draft with the current best docs links and what we’re changing.

[13:29] Ben Carter: Great.

[13:31] Sabrina James: And Jordan, if you can share one sample 429 response headers and one sample streaming disconnect log, I can confirm the correct handling and then we’ll send a recommended pattern.

[13:41] Jordan Lee: Yeah, we can do that. We have request IDs.

[13:44] Sabrina James: Perfect.

[13:46] Ben Carter: While we have time, can we walk through the exact moment you got stuck at “first request”? Like step-by-step.

[13:54] Maya Desai: Sure. We created an account, created a key. Then quickstart said set env var, run curl. Curl failed. We tried again. We realized we were using the wrong endpoint.

[14:07] Jordan Lee: Then we got a 200 with a completion. Great. Then we tried to integrate into our service. Our service uses streaming. The streaming example we found was for a different SDK version and it didn’t compile.

[14:20] Wei Chen: Oh that’s bad.

[14:21] Jordan Lee: Yeah. It was like a method name changed. So then we did fetch manually.

[14:27] Sabrina James: That’s on us; we should version the snippets.

[14:31] Jordan Lee: Then with fetch, it worked but sometimes it dropped. And we didn’t know if we should retry. Then we turned on a small load test and got 429.

[14:43] Maya Desai: And at that point we were like, okay, we need guidance.

[14:47] Ben Carter: Yup.

[14:48] Priya Natarajan: The big ask is: don’t make us discover these problems by accident.

[14:55] Ben Carter: Totally.

[15:00] Ben Carter: Okay I’m going to ask one pricing-ish question just to calibrate. If you need higher rate limits for pilot, is that something you’d be willing to move to a paid tier for quickly?

[15:11] Priya Natarajan: Maybe. We’d need an estimate and we’d need to be confident it’s stable.

[15:16] Ben Carter: Totally. I’ll send info on what the next tier looks like and we can also talk about Dedicated later if you want predictable throughput.

[15:25] Maya Desai: Dedicated is later. Right now we just want Hosted to not surprise us.

[15:30] Ben Carter: Understood.

[15:33] Wei Chen: On the dashboard lag: we should probably document the expected freshness. There’s like “request logs” which is near real time and “usage/billing” which can lag.

[15:44] Jordan Lee: Yes please. Because we used billing as a debugging tool.

[15:48] Ben Carter: Yeah, don’t do that.

[15:50] Jordan Lee: Now we know.

[15:52] Sabrina James: For production, we also recommend emitting your own structured logs with request IDs and latency. Do you have observability set up already?

[16:01] Jordan Lee: We do. Datadog. We can hook it.

[16:04] Sabrina James: Great. We can show where to grab the request ID and put it in your spans.

[16:09] Maya Desai: Add it to the checklist.

[16:11] Ben Carter: Noted.

[16:13] Priya Natarajan: So what happens next? Like, can we see the draft checklist?

[16:18] Ben Carter: Yes. Wei can send draft copy and links. Sabrina can send recommended defaults for TS, especially around retries/timeouts and streaming.

[16:28] Maya Desai: Great.

[16:30] Jordan Lee: And can you clarify the 429s—like, do you have a way to show current quota and “you are at 80%”?

[16:37] Ben Carter: There is a limits view. But it’s not obvious, and it’s not proactive.

[16:42] Priya Natarajan: That’s exactly it. We want proactive.

[16:46] Ben Carter: Yep.

[16:48] (brief silence)

[16:50] Ben Carter: Anything else you want to make sure we fix?

[16:54] Maya Desai: Honestly, the copy. Like, don’t call it “go live” if it’s not actually the go-live steps. It should be “hello world” and “production launch.”

[17:05] Wei Chen: That’s good feedback.

[17:06] Sabrina James: And the SDK should make the safe thing easy. Defaults matter.

[17:11] Jordan Lee: Yeah.

[17:12] Ben Carter: Okay. I think we’ve got what we need. Before we wrap, let’s recap action items.

[17:18] Ben Carter: One: Maya/Jordan, you’ll send us request IDs and sample 401/403, 429, and one streaming disconnect example.

[17:27] Jordan Lee: Yep.

[17:28] Ben Carter: Two: Wei will send you a consolidated checklist draft with canonical docs links—auth, env var, first request, streaming production guidance, quotas/budgets, usage dashboard expectations.

[17:41] Wei Chen: Yes.

[17:42] Ben Carter: Three: Sabrina will send a production-ready TS snippet and general recommended timeouts/retries, including streaming caveats.

[17:51] Sabrina James: Yep.

[17:52] Ben Carter: And four: I’ll follow up with plan options to avoid rate limit surprises for your pilot.

[17:58] Priya Natarajan: Great.

[18:00] Ben Carter: Cool. Thanks everyone. We’ll follow up by early next week.

[18:05] Maya Desai: Thanks.

[18:06] Jordan Lee: Thanks.

[18:07] Priya Natarajan: Thank you.

(end)
